checks: Assume no limit affine component vanishes identically on the limiting plane. A nonzero tangential gradient keeps a positive lower norm after projection to the moving planes. Because the component is positive on the sections, its sublevel portion lies in a slab of width ≤t/γ_r, with bounded cross-sectional area inside the common outer ball. This gives O(t), including an interval when d=2.

A component with zero tangential gradient is constant on the limit plane. If infinitely many sections are nonempty, convergence of bounded section points and positivity give a nonnegative constant. Under the assumed absence of a zero restriction it is positive; coefficient and plane convergence make the current restrictions uniformly positive on all late nonempty sections. If the sequence is eventually empty, no defect remains.

Union over the fixed finite list gives the same O(t) sublevel rate for the minimum. The anchor lemma's layer-cake/truncation argument applies to that bound, so its contrapositive yields a zero component on the whole plane. Since L is positive inside K the component is nonconstant when it vanishes on the plane; its zero set equals the plane and its gradient is parallel to u.

The nonzero measure defect is supported on the limiting fiber and plane. Each component is nonnegative on K; the exposed face in the plane is entirely in L=0, and the predecessor's inverse-integral criterion bounds its dimension. Positive versus negative proportionality makes the captured halfspace include all of K versus only that face.

In the example, s=x+y has fiber length in x equal to s and Jacobian one. Integrating s/(s−a+η)=1+(a−η)/(s−a+η) gives the printed inverse bound since 0≤a−η≤1/m and the logarithm is at most m·log 2. For m≥2 the cut is proper, has raw coarea a+η², and L_m=η(1+η) there.

The weighted mass is (a+η²)[m log 2−log(1+η)]. The leading coefficient is 1+m4^(−m), and log(1+η)≤η, giving convergence to log 2. The supports converge to the zero vertex. Reversing the normal changes neither coarea nor weight; rescaling the parameter by bounded-log factors changes the integral by at most a constant times the vanishing coarea. Fraction arithmetic checked the exact rational ranges and coefficients for m=2 through 100.
